sections.heading: Section 1: Sector Area Formula & Single Curves

questions.q: Which integral formula calculates the area of a region bounded by the polar curve $r = f(\theta)$ from $\alpha$ to $\beta$?
questions.answer: Polar area is the sum of infinitesimal circular sectors with area $dA = \frac{1}{2} r^2 d\theta$.

questions.q: Find the area enclosed by the circle $r = 4\sin\theta$ for $\theta \in [0, \pi]$.
What is the area enclosed by one petal of the four-petal rose $r = 2\cos(2\theta)$?
questions.answer: One petal spans from $\theta = -\pi/4$ to $\pi/4$. Area $= \frac{1}{2} \int_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4} 4\cos^2(2\theta) d\theta = 2 \int_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4} \frac{1 + \cos(4\theta)}{2} d\theta = [\theta + \frac{\sin(4\theta)}{4}]_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4} = \frac{\pi}{4} - (-\frac{\pi}{4}) = \frac{\pi}{2}$.

sections.heading: Section 2: Area Between Two Polar Curves

questions.q: Which integral represents the area inside $r = R(\theta)$ and outside $r = r(\theta)$?
questions.answer: Area is difference of sectors: $\frac{1}{2} \int (R^2 - r^2) d\theta$.

questions.q: Find the points of intersection of $r = 3$ and $r = 6\cos\theta$.
Set up the integral for the area inside $r = 6\cos\theta$ and outside $r = 3$.
questions.answer: Outer curve is $6\cos\theta$, inner curve is $3$. Formula: $\frac{1}{2} \int_{-\pi/3}^{\pi/3} (36\cos^2\theta - 9) d\theta$.

sections.heading: Section 3: Common Interior of Two Curves

questions.q: How is the common interior area of two overlapping polar curves calculated when the boundary changes?
choices: By finding the intersection angle and splitting the region into separate single-curve integrals
By subtracting the outer curve from the inner curve
By integrating the product of the two curves
By averaging the two individual areas
questions.answer: When rays from the origin transition from hitting one curve to hitting another, the area must be split at the intersection angle into separate integrals.

questions.q: Find the area inside both $r = 2$ and $r = 4\sin\theta$ in the first quadrant.
questions.answer: Intersection: $4\sin\theta = 2 \Rightarrow \sin\theta = 1/2 \Rightarrow \theta = \pi/6$. From $0$ to $\pi/6$, bound is $4\sin\theta$; from $\pi/6$ to $\pi/2$, bound is $2$. Sum yields $\frac{4\pi}{3} - \sqrt{3}$.

questions.q: Why does the pole require special care when finding intersection points of polar curves?
choices: Because $r = 0$ corresponds to the same physical point (the origin) regardless of the angle $\theta$
Because the area at the pole is infinite
It does not require special care
questions.answer: The origin can be reached by two curves at entirely different values of $\theta$, so setting $f(\theta) = g(\theta)$ may fail to detect an intersection at the pole.

questions.q: What is the range of $\theta$ required to trace the limaçon $r = 2 + \cos\theta$ exactly once?
questions.answer: For a limaçon without loops ($r = a + b\cos\theta$ with $a > b$), the curve is traced exactly once as $\theta$ traverses $[0, 2\pi]$.

questions.q: Find the total area enclosed by the cardioid $r = 2(1 + \cos\theta)$.
How many times is the circle $r = \sin(2\theta)$ traced over $[0, 2\pi]$?
choices: It is a 4-petal rose traced once over $[0, 2\pi]$
It is a circle traced twice
questions.answer: $r = \sin(2\theta)$ is an eight-petal or four-petal curve (four distinct petals) traced once completely as $\theta$ increases from $0$ to $2\pi$.
